events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. events.excerpt: A growing class of protocols needs to persist one tiny fact per event, forever: this nullifier is spent, this nonce is used, this session share is settled. Privacy pools write a nullifier per withdrawal. Unordered nonce schemes (Permit2’s nonceBitmap , EIP-4337-style two-dimensional nonces) write replay flags because they cannot guarantee sequenced nonces. Machine-scale settlement (DePIN connectivity, bandwidth, compute) writes a mark per settled session. Call all of it what it is: replay protection, and its cost is pure storage. ZK batching has made the compute side nearly free: one proof verifies thousands of signatures or membership checks at flat cost. The flags are what no longer compress. The progression every protocol rediscovers. Worst case, and still the most common shape: mapping(bytes32 => bool) used; // one flag, one slot // every flag: ~22,100 gas (20,000 zero-to-nonzero + 2,100 cold access), state forever This is what nullifier sets look like: the key is a hash, so no two flags ever share a slot, and nothing amortizes. events.excerpt: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022 , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver . In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. events.excerpt: tl;dr Open-bidding with random deadline (candle auctions) and few auction participants can lead to higher bidder profits than sealed-bid auctions. This is already true in a one-shot auction without explicit coordination or collusion. For the Ethereum builder-market post-Glamsterdam, I conjecture that this gives current participants a strong incentive to maintain the current open-bid auction by restricting outside bidding and per-missioning participation in relay auctions. In this post I want to formalize a piece of folk knowledge which I think is well-known among many searchers, builders and other participants of the MEV ecosystem: Open bidding auctions with a random deadline and few participants tend to give those participants more payoff than a sealed auction. On a high level, the logic is straightforward. Uncertainty about the auction deadline (in the case of PoS Ethereum through heterogeneous proposer behavior (timing games) and locations) creates for equally fast bidders with equal value a quasi-lottery: Bidders can outbid each other in small increments and whoever manages to place the last bid before the auction ends wins. events.excerpt: Summary Rollups scaled by moving execution off the L1, but the authentication part of every transaction still goes to the L1. That makes data the likely bottleneck for L2 scaling in the PQ era, even with more blobs. PQ signatures are far larger than ECDSA, so if every L2 user switched to one, signatures would make up 99% of transaction data and the transfers that fit in 6 blobs would fall from about 6,600 to 155. ZK applications have it worse, since a single PQ proof usually does not fit in 3 blobs. Either way, the bottleneck is that the cost of checking trust grows with the number of users. An L2 can cut this cost by adopting EIP-8288: signatures and proofs move out of transactions, and the statements of many blocks are bundled into one leanVM aggregate proof posted to the L1. A transaction authenticated with leanSPHINCS then compresses to 100 to 129 bytes, close to an ECDSA transaction. A 32-core machine (AWS c7a.8xlarge) can prove up to 170 leanSPHINCS signatures per second on a 2-second chain. At that load, the 2,040 leanSPHINCS transactions arriving per L1 block fit in 2.8 to 3.3 blobs on average, calculated from the measured aggregate size and compression ratio. events.excerpt: Most key-compromise defenses today (smart wallets, ERC-7579 modules, social recovery, EIP-7702 delegation) enforce policy in the account’s code. ERC-8403 continues this: spend limits and unlock times are authorities committed under the account’s root. I’d like to probe a different placement: enforcing rate limits at the asset : the token contract for ERC-20s, and eventually the protocol itself for native ETH. Motivation. Account-level policy only binds while the account’s code is in the transfer path. Two gaps: Allowances : a contract holding an existing transferFrom approval moves tokens without re-entering the wallet’s validation logic, so a wallet-level daily limit does not bind. Delegation replacement : under EIP-7702, the compromised EOA key can re-delegate and strip the policy that was supposed to contain it. An asset-level check binds every balance-reducing path ( transfer , transferFrom , burns) regardless of which application initiated it, and survives delegation changes. Sketch (details negotiable, that is the point of the thread): Optional per-account spending limit (rolling window) enforced where balances change. events.excerpt: Abstract PropAMMs are on-chain venues whose prices are set by a single maker. The maker pushes quote state on-chain, and fills read that state. We decoded 92,627 fills on nine Ethereum PropAMMs over 30 days (10 September to 9 October 2026) from execution data. We priced the 69,827 WETH/stablecoin fills against Binance one-second trades. Three of the registry venues accept maker state only if it is stamped with the current block’s timestamp. Their fills always execute against an update in the same block. Takers pay about 0.45 bp at the fill, on every one of the 30 days. Over the following five minutes the price does not move in their favour on average, in any taker class: there is no sign of adverse selection. Of fills after a CEX move of more than 0.5 bp in the preceding 12 seconds, 78.5% trade against it. The PropAMM quote follows the CEX in the same block, while Uniswap lags. Arbitrage contracts and routers use the PropAMM as the fresh side of a trade against a stale AMM. Fills are priced no later than their block’s sealing, which relays received 0.1 to 3.1 s after the slot start on the two days measured. Markouts change by under 0.1 bp across that range. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar , TÜRKTRUST , and TrustWave ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. events.excerpt: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall ( WAF ), caching , bot management , and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. The goal is to prevent stolen ATOM from being moved further during major security incidents, without halting the entire network, while leaving final decisions to decentralized governance. events.excerpt: Digital signatures control who can spend funds, issue commands and authorize requests. Widely used schemes rely on factoring or discrete logarithms, assumptions threatened by Shor’s quantum algorithm. The post-quantum transition therefore reaches the mechanism used to establish authority itself. Post-quantum signatures provide replacements with different security assumptions, key sizes, signature sizes and verification costs. Applications that also prove execution must express that verification in their proof arithmetic. Signatureless authorization takes a direct proof-of-knowledge approach. An authority publishes a commitment to a reusable secret. Each action is authorized by a freshly randomized zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of that secret, bound to the requested action. The central security problem is safe reuse: an adversary can collect valid proofs, adapt later requests to earlier responses and attempt to authorize a fresh request. The funds are now held at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000DA0 . The funds can only be moved by an ArbitrumDAO Governance vote, which will be coordinated with relevant parties. Key point: Funds associated with the Binance exploit are frozen on Arbitrum One. No other user’s funds or applications were affected.
